extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners and general readers interested in media/journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices for investigative journalism—especially audio/podcast reporting—focused on source verification, fact-checking, editorial oversight, transparency, and accountability when a central source's claims are in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of source claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times 'failed to push hard enough to verify Chaudhry's claims' and 'did not have evidence Chaudhry had ever been to Syria.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors must obtain powerful, corroborating evidence for extraordinary claims (travel, membership in violent groups, participation in killings) rather than relying on a subject's on-record or on-tape statements. Pursue documentary, official, or independent corroboration before presenting such claims as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking and accuracy standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The series 'did not meet its standards for accuracy or fact-checking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work must meet the publication's stated accuracy and fact-checking requirements; if core elements cannot be verified they should not be published as presented. When failures occur, they require public correction, editor's notes, or retraction as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and avoiding undue deference to reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors 'relied on Callimachi's judgment' and were 'deferential to an ambitious audio investigative team presenting a compelling narrative yarn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not defer solely to a reporter's reputation or narrative enthusiasm. Editorial leadership must independently scrutinize verification, demand documentation, and push back when reporting relies on weak or contradictory evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about compelling narratives (avoid narrative seduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'We were so in love with it that when we saw evidence that maybe he was a fabulist, ... we didn't listen hard enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compelling or dramatic narrative should not trump skeptical inquiry. Newsrooms must guard against letting storytelling momentum obscure or excuse lapses in verification and critical editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration from official sources must be based on hard evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporting 'relied on corroboration from colleagues ... that U.S. and Canadian intelligence officials harbored a suspicion' but 'it wasn't clear whether those officials relied on hard evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondhand assertions that officials 'suspected' something are insufficient; corroboration from intelligence or government sources must be traceable to concrete evidence, documents, or verifiable testimony rather than hearsay or belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, corrections, and public accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times is 'posting an editor's note atop each element of Caliphate' and discussing returning awards and other corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When failures occur, news organizations should be transparent with readers (editor's notes, corrections, retractions), explain what went wrong, and take visible remedial steps (correct the record, return awards where appropriate) to rebuild trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassignment or limiting beats after major errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper says Rukmini Callimachi 'will no longer cover terrorism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant lapses in judgment or repeated verification failures may warrant reassigning reporters or restricting beat responsibilities to preserve credibility and ensure appropriate oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of identity for anonymous/pseudonymous sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaudhry spoke 'under the pseudonym Abu Huzayfah,' complicating verification of his claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a central source uses a pseudonym or anonymity, newsrooms must take added steps to verify identity and background before building a narrative around that person's assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding rigorously to red flags and contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Murphy found Callimachi and editors 'repeatedly failed to push hard enough to verify' and the man's account was 'riddled with holes and contradictions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should treat contradictions and red flags as triggers for deeper investigation rather than rationalize or reframe timelines to make facts fit the narrative. Pursue alternative explanations and additional sources until inconsistencies are resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in relying on social media and real-time analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Callimachi 'in posting real-time analyses on social media ... has helped to cement her reputation' but social-media-derived claims require scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real-time or social-media-based analysis can inform reporting but must be corroborated through standard reporting practices; social posts or early commentary should not substitute for verified evidence in investigative pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting purchased or third-party materials and documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times 'disclosed it had bought video footage' and had past instances where 'a scoop required a subsequent editor's note and a full follow-up story to address doubts about the veracity of the documents she relied upon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using purchased footage, third-party documents, or material from intermediaries, newsrooms must verify provenance and authenticity and be prepared to follow up if doubts emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: External recognition does not substitute for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Caliphate 'won a Peabody' and was a 'finalist for the Pulitzer Prize' yet core reporting was later retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards and acclaim do not validate the accuracy of reporting; editorial standards and verification should remain the primary criteria for judging journalistic work regardless of external honors.
